references.text: The same chapter describes the skinning and dismemberment of the sacrificial animal, which is part of the same offering process
Parallel text describing the priest's task of placing the pieces, the head, and the fat on the wood that is burning on the altar
Moses dismembered the ram and burned the head, the pieces, and the fat, demonstrating the practical execution of this regulation
Describes how the burnt offering was given to Aaron piece by piece, along with the head, and he burned it on the altar
Instruction to cut the ram into pieces, wash the entrails and the feet, and place them upon the pieces and the head
Highlights the common theological principle that the fat is 'the Lord's food' which is burned on the altar.
Confirms that the rule to burn all fat applies across different types of offerings (burnt offering and sin offering).
Contrasts complete combustion (burnt offering) with a symbolic memorial portion to show the breadth of sacrificial rituals.
Emphasizes the universal principle that all fat belongs to the Lord and must be burned on the altar.
Explains the theological basis for why the fat in Lev 1:12 is burned: it belongs to the Lord as a 'fire offering'.
Confirms that the principle of burning fat on the altar applies even in the special context of the Day of Atonement.
Shows that the principle of combustion on the altar is common to different categories of offerings (burnt and guilt offerings).
